segments.original: Hollywood still seemed healthy in the years immediately after the war: 1946 was the year of highest movie attendance, beating the record set in 1939. segments.original: A drama about the return of three war veterans, the film addresses the complexity of the men's lives, the memories of combat that haunted them and the challenges their families and friends had to face. It ends on a relatively melancholy note, but there is no escaping the difficulties each of the characters will have to face, reflecting the sense of unease that pervaded much of the United States.

segments.original: Hollywood's shift toward darker territory had begun earlier, with the arrival of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) in 1947. The committee was charged with investigating the infiltration of communist sympathizers among the film elite and, as a result, more than 250 members of the Hollywood community were barred from working in film, while many others were forced to name communists.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: One of the most famous informers was Elia Kazan (1909-2003), whose film On the Waterfront (1954) seems like a response to his critics, with a mob informer (played by Marlon Brando) as its protagonist. Unlike Kazan, Ring Lardner Jr. (1915-2000), one of the many blacklisted screenwriters, cited for contempt during his 1947 testimony, told the committee: "I could answer the question (...) but if I did, I would hate myself in the morning." Writer Lillian Hellman was more incisive. In 1948, she wrote: "Naturally, men frightened to make pictures about the American Negro, men who only in the last year allowed the word Jew to be spoken in a picture, who took more than ten years to make an anti-fascist picture, these are frightened men and you pick frightened men to frighten first. Judas goats, they lead the others to the slaughter for you".

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Hollywood was terrified by the investigations, which cast a shadow over the industry. In a submissive reaction, several studios produced anticommunist films, among them My Son John (1952) and Pickup on South Street (1953). Even children's films, such as the adaptation The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T. (1953), based on a book by Dr. Seuss, were considered to have communist connotations. The fad passed, but the damage caused by the investigations, along with the ever-growing hole in the studios' coffers, the impact of television and a more diverse audience less interested in what the studios had to offer, marked the end of the golden age of the Hollywood studios.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Television was a cheap form of entertainment. In 1940, there were 3,785 television sets in the United States. By 1960, nine out of 10 homes had a television. After the initial investment, these sets gave families endless hours of entertainment. Recognizing that audiences still loved the movies, the television networks began to compete with the studios, creating series that copied Hollywood's most popular genres. Success came so quickly that smaller studios went bankrupt and the networks bought up their properties and used them to film their own mass entertainment products.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A remake of a silent epic released in 1925, Ben-Hur was part of a series of spectacular films that were huge box office hits in the 1950s. After Quo Vadis (1951), The Robe (1953) and The Ten Commandments (1956), Ben-Hur was hailed as the greatest epic of all epics. But it is also remembered for a sarcastic quip ("Loved Ben. Hated Hur") as much as for its achievements. What prompted the criticism was that director William Wyler adopted the theory of Cecil B. DeMille (1881-1959) that audiences of biblical films allowed themselves to enjoy orgies and violence only because, in the end, divine wrath fell upon the wicked.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A more sophisticated filmmaker than DeMille, Wyler felt that it was not enough to bring the temple down on the villains. So the strong, simple story of Judah Ben-Hur (Charlton Heston), the noble Jew betrayed and enslaved by his false Roman friend Messala (Stephen Boyd), alternates crowd-pleasing action scenes with "inspirational" encounters with Christ, which allow Heston to deal with religious matters. Subsequent sword-and-sandal epics, from Spartacus (1960) to Gladiator (2000), toned down the preaching and turned up the violence, suggesting that a lesson had been learned. Still, while Heston and Boyd shine on their chariots, audiences can't help loving Ben-Hur. The film was the biggest commercial hit of the year and held the record for Oscars until Titanic (1997).

Paramount Pictures, Inc., 334 US 131 - put an end to years of vertical integration, under which the studios could own the theaters where their films were shown. The ruling also restricted block booking and the fixing of ticket prices. The impact of the decision shook Hollywood, wrecking a system that had prevailed for three decades. The new rules did significant damage to the increasingly empty coffers of this film district.

segments.original: On the other hand, the end of film censorship gave filmmakers more freedom of expression in the United States. In 1952, the Supreme Court overturned a 1915 ruling, finally granting films the protection of free speech guaranteed by the First Amendment. segments.original: The world and cinema were about to change. The rebellious teenagers of the 1950s became the bikers of the 1960s; the fun-loving hero of many screwball comedies, Cary Grant (1904-1986), was fighting to save himself in North by Northwest (1959); handsome Tony Curtis (1925-2010) subverted his image in 1957 by playing press agent Sidney Falco in the noir-tinged Sweet Smell of Success (1957); American directors were beginning to be influenced by French directors; and, in reaction to social and political upheaval, a new era of cinematic violence and liberal productions was about to take shape. Hollywood's golden age was over, and cinema awaited its bold and uncertain future.
